title: The Oracle Against Babylon and the Day of the LORD
summary: The first of Isaiah's oracles against the nations is aimed at Babylon. The LORD summons an army from far away, and the Day of the LORD breaks over the world with darkened skies, terror, and the humbling of the proud. God stirs up the Medes against Babylon, and the jewel of the kingdoms is overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah, left to wild animals and never inhabited again.
story: Chapter 12 closed the first section of Isaiah with a song that sent God's praise out to the nations. Chapters 13 to 23 now turn to those nations directly in a series of oracles: Babylon, Assyria, Philistia, Moab, Damascus, Cush, Egypt, Edom, Arabia, and Tyre, with a word to Jerusalem set among them. The collection makes a single claim: the God of little Judah rules every empire and city-state on its map. It begins with Babylon, which in Isaiah's day was not yet the great power it would become but which would, a century later, destroy Jerusalem and carry Judah into exile. By opening the oracles here, the book announces at the start that the empire that will one day seem invincible stands under God's judgment.
historical:
Isaiah prophesied from about 740 to 700 BC, when Assyria, not Babylon, dominated the Near East. Babylon was an ancient and revered city in southern Mesopotamia, but in this period it was usually under Assyrian control and often in revolt. A Chaldean leader named Merodach-baladan (who appears in Isaiah 39) seized Babylon's throne around 721 BC and held it for about a decade, and briefly again around 703 BC, before being driven out. The Chaldeans (verse 19) were tribal peoples of southern Babylonia whose leaders later founded the Neo-Babylonian Empire. In 689 BC the Assyrian king Sennacherib captured and devastated Babylon. After Assyria collapsed, the Babylonians under Nabopolassar and his son Nebuchadnezzar became the new empire, with Medes as their allies in the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC. The Medes were an Iranian people east of Assyria whose kingdom was absorbed by Cyrus the Persian around 550 BC.

The oracle's setting and fulfillment are debated. Many critical scholars date the chapter to the exile in the sixth century BC, when Babylon ruled and the rising Medes and Persians were its obvious threat. Others, including many who hold that Isaiah wrote it, point to the eighth-century setting: Babylon was already a byword for pride, Isaiah elsewhere foresees exile to Babylon (39:6-7), and some think the oracle was first heard against the background of Sennacherib's destruction of the city. A further complication is that when Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC it fell with little fighting and remained a major city. Its decline was gradual: it was damaged in revolts under the Persian kings, lost importance when the Seleucid rulers founded Seleucia on the Tigris around 300 BC, and was largely deserted by the early centuries AD. Some readers therefore see the prophecy fulfilled over centuries rather than in one day; others read verses 19 to 22 as the stock language of total ruin used in ancient curses, whose point is that pride falls, not a timetable.
cultural:
The heading calls this a burden or oracle (Hebrew massa), the title used for most of the oracles in chapters 13 to 23. Oracles against foreign nations were a recognized form in Israel and its neighbors; Amos 1 and 2, Jeremiah 46 to 51, and Ezekiel 25 to 32 contain similar collections. They were spoken in Jerusalem, and their first audience was Judah, not the foreign kings, so their message was also a warning to God's people not to trust or fear the empires.

The picture of desolation uses the ordinary signs of a ruined city in the ancient world. Once walls and canals fell into disrepair, the fields of southern Mesopotamia turned to salt flats and desert scrub, and ruined mounds (tells) became the haunt of jackals, owls, ostriches, and wild goats. Assyrian royal inscriptions and treaty curses use similar images of a city given over to wild animals. The mention of Ophir in verse 12 refers to a distant land famous for fine gold, visited by Solomon's ships (1 Kings 9:28), whose exact location is unknown.
literary: The chapter moves from the local to the cosmic and back. Verses 2 to 5 are a battle summons: a banner is raised and the LORD of Hosts musters his army. Verses 6 to 16 widen into the Day of the LORD, when God judges the whole world, with stars darkened, heavens shaken, and people writhing like a woman in labor. Verses 17 to 22 narrow again to Babylon and the Medes. The mixing of the particular and the universal is deliberate: Babylon's fall becomes a sample of how God deals with every proud power. Repeated words hold it together, especially pride (verses 3, 11, and 19) and burning anger (verses 9 and 13). The comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah (verse 19) recalls the Bible's archetype of total overthrow in Genesis 19.

outline.t: The heading: an oracle against Babylon
The LORD musters an army from far away
The Day of the LORD is near: terror and anguish
Cosmic darkness and the humbling of the proud
Flight and slaughter in the conquered land
The Medes against Babylon and its lasting desolation

doctrines.note: The Day of the LORD is God's intervention to put down evil and pride. God punishes the world for its evil and brings down the arrogant, and no empire is exempt.
God calls the armies of foreign peoples his own warriors and stirs up the Medes. Nations that act for their own reasons still serve purposes they do not know.
The sin most named here is pride and arrogance, the haughtiness of the ruthless. Babylon's glory becomes the reason for its fall.

words.note: Massa, an oracle or burden. It comes from the verb to lift or carry, and scholars debate whether it means a pronouncement lifted up by the voice or a heavy load laid on the prophet. It heads most of the oracles in chapters 13 to 23, marking them as a single collection.

Yom, day. In the phrase the Day of the LORD (verses 6 and 9) it names the time when God acts decisively to judge and to set things right. Amos 5 had already warned that Israel should not assume this day would be good news for them. Here it falls on Babylon and the whole world.

Maday, the Medes, an Iranian people from the highlands east of Mesopotamia. They helped the Babylonians bring down Assyria in 612 BC and were later joined to the Persian Empire under Cyrus. Their naming here, rather than the Persians, is one clue scholars use in dating the oracle.

Gaon, pride or majesty. The word can describe God's majesty positively, but here (verses 11 and 19) it is human self-exaltation. Babylon is called the glory of the pride of the Chaldeans, the very thing that marks it for judgment.

christ: Jesus used the language of this chapter when he spoke of the end of the age: the sun darkened, the moon not giving its light, the stars falling (Matthew 24:29, drawing on Isaiah 13:10 and 34:4). The New Testament also takes up Babylon as a name for every proud power that sets itself against God. Revelation 17 and 18 describe the fall of Babylon the great, echoing Isaiah's desolate city haunted by wild creatures. These are not predictions of Jesus in the direct sense; they show that the pattern Isaiah saw in Babylon's fall is the pattern Christ will complete when he judges the world and brings in his kingdom. Christians also read the Day of the LORD in light of the cross, where God's judgment on sin fell on the Son, so that the day of wrath can become a day of rescue for those who trust him.

hard.q: How can a prophecy from God describe infants dashed to pieces and wives ravished?
hard.a: Verses 15 to 18 are among the hardest lines in the prophets. The difficulty is real and should not be softened. Several things help in reading them. First, the prophet is describing what ancient warfare actually did; Assyrian and Babylonian armies routinely committed such atrocities, and Babylon itself would do them to Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC (compare Lamentations 5:11 and Psalm 137). The oracle announces that the violence Babylon inflicted will return on it, not that God approves the soldiers' cruelty. Second, elsewhere Isaiah and the other prophets condemn the conquerors' brutality even when they serve as God's instruments (Isaiah 10:5-15, 47:6). Third, many interpreters note that the Bible speaks of God giving people over to the consequences of their deeds, working through human evil without being its author. None of this makes the passage easy, and honest readers have always found it disturbing. Its disturbing force is part of its warning: when empires sow violence, they reap it.

questions: Babylon is called the jewel of the kingdoms and brought down for its pride. What forms of national or personal pride does this chapter challenge today?
These oracles were first heard in Jerusalem, not in Babylon. What did it mean for Judah to hear that the coming superpower stood under God's judgment?
How do you respond to a God who judges the proud and the ruthless? Is it more comforting or more unsettling, and why?
